geeknews.title: Microsoft, 대규모 장애 이후 ‘Code Red’ 선언…내부 메모로 드러난 대응 문제
geeknews.summary: Microsoft가 24시간 서비스 장애 이후 재발 방지와 복구 체계 개선을 최우선으로 추진하는 ‘Code Red’에 돌입함. 내부 메모에는 엔지니어링 체계와...
geeknews.text:
Microsoft가 24시간 서비스 장애 이후 재발 방지와 복구 체계 개선을 최우선으로 추진하는 ‘Code Red’에 돌입 함. 내부 메모에는 엔지니어링 체계와 장애 대응 과정의 취약점이 드러남
Exchange Online 역사상 고객 영향이 가장 컸던 장애로, Outlook, Teams, Copilot 등 Microsoft 365 서비스와 여러 국가의 정부, 금융 거래 업체, 항공사 통신에 차질이 발생함
원인은 7월에 도입된 뒤 발견되지 않은 Windows 확장성 결함 이며, Microsoft는 사이버 활동이나 AI 에이전트와는 무관하다고 밝힘
대응 인력이 Teams 채팅방 11개에서 메시지 1만 1,000건 이상 을 주고받았지만, 진단 정보가 여러 시스템에 흩어져 가설과 의사결정을 한눈에 파악하기 어려웠음
과부하 시 일부 요청을 제한하고 지역별로 트래픽을 분리 하는 등 복구 체계를 개선해, 향후 장애를 전 세계에서 1시간 안에 해결하는 것 을 목표로 함. AI 에이전트로 진단 데이터 분석도 지원할 계획임
24시간 장애와 Code Red 발동
Reuters가 확인한 내부 메모에 따르면 Microsoft는 대규모 서비스 장애의 예방과 대응 방식 을 전면 개선하기 위해 Code Red를 선언함
Code Red는 중대한 위기에 사용하는 최고 수준의 긴급 대응으로, 이번에는 엔지니어링과 운영 관행의 취약점 개선을 최우선 과제로 삼음
11월 12~13일 장애 는 클라우드 이메일 서비스 Exchange Online뿐 아니라 Outlook, Teams, AI 비서 Copilot과 다른 Microsoft 365 제품에도 영향을 줌
호주, 일본, 미국 등의 정부가 영향을 받았고, 금융 거래 업체의 업무가 지연됐으며 항공사 통신에도 차질이 발생함
이로 인해 핵심 디지털 인프라의 취약성 에 대한 우려가 커짐
Microsoft가 지목한 원인은 7월에 도입된 Windows 확장성 결함 으로, 장애 전까지 발견되지 않았음
사이버 활동이나 AI 에이전트와는 관련이 없다고 밝혔으며, CEO Satya Nadella는 공개 사과함
M365 Core 사장 Jason Henderson 의 직원 메모에 따르면 이번 사고는 Exchange Online 역사상 고객 영향이 가장 컸던 사고임
이처럼 많은 고객이 이처럼 오랫동안 이메일을 사용하지 못한 전례가 없으며, Code Red 관련 작업은 팀의 최우선 업무임
분산된 진단 정보와 혼란스러운 대응
M365 Core와 AI 에이전트용 업무 인텔리전스 플랫폼 Work IQ를 총괄하는 Amanda Silver 부사장의 내부 메모에 따르면, 장애 대응 당시 엔지니어들은 ‘전장의 안개’ 같은 혼란 속에서 일함

Copilot, Agents and Platform 담당 수석 부사장 Charles Lamanna 는 Code Red 검토 회의에서 해당 구성 요소가 겪은 장애를 “약 10년 치의 허용 가능한 장애”에 비유함

안드로이드 자동화를 하다 보면 adb shell input text 로 한글이 들어가지 않는 문제를 만나게 됩니다. 이 명령은 ASCII 만 보낼 수 있어서, 한글·이모지 같은 글자는 넣을 수 없습니다.
저희도 테스트 폰에서 한글 입력을 자동화하다가 같은 문제를 만나서, 작은 도구를 만들어 공개했습니다.
구성: 키보드 화면이 없는 입력기 앱(권한 없음, 네트워크 없음)과 PC 쪽 파이썬 스크립트
동작: 스크립트가 이 입력기로 바꾼 뒤 지금 선택된 입력칸에 글자를 넣고, 끝나면 원래 키보드로 항상 되돌립니다
사용 예: printf '안녕하세요' | python3 host/ime_input.py --pkg com.example.app
안전하게 쓰려고 정한 것들입니다.
비밀번호 칸에는 넣지 않습니다
엔터·보내기는 누르지 않습니다
본문은 표준입력으로만 받고, 출력에는 길이와 해시만 남깁니다
지금 열린 앱·입력칸과 맞을 때만 넣어서, 다른 앱에 잘못 들어가지 않게 했습니다(웹 입력칸은 앱 단위까지만 확인합니다)
한계도 있습니다. 안드로이드 14 이상에서만 되고, 안드로이드 15 기기 몇 대에서만 시험했습니다. 크롬 같은 웹 입력칸에도 들어가지만, 넣은 글을 다시 읽어 볼 수 없어 화면 캡처로 확인해야 합니다. 한 번에 2000자까지 넣을 수 있습니다.
QA 자동화, 휴대폰을 다루는 AI 에이전트, 한글 테스트 자동화에 쓸 수 있습니다. 라이선스는 Apache-2.0 입니다. 다른 기기에서 써 보신 결과를 알려 주시면 큰 도움이 됩니다.

hn.title: Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
hn.text:
← All news November 27, 2026
Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
All the sites we contacted took action; but the larger consumer web ecosystem should be prepared to mitigate these attack vectors
A card-skimming script was planted on the online stores of Lascana, Samsonite, American Tourister, Revolve and FWRD in the week before Black Friday. After our reports to affected companies, all have had the script removed (on November 24th or 25th) ahead of Black Friday. We observed it in action on one of the five websites: Lascana, where it sent our test card's details to a 3rd party. We believe the script was built to take a card number, expiry and security code, along with a user's name, address, phone and email, and send them to malefactors as a user entered their payment credentials. It did this before the store checked the payment, so a card could be taken even if the order was declined or cancelled, and nothing would look wrong to the shopper. Across all of these sites, we do not know how many, if any, shopper details or payment credentials may have been captured.
Which sites were affected
Consumer site
Delivery method
Status at time of publication
Lascana www.lascana.com
Altered Quorum * marketing pixel
Both Lascana and Quorum replied and removed the code on the 24th,
see details below
Samsonite
shop.samsonite.com
Edited Seers † cookie-banner setting
Neither party replied to us, but the code was removed on November
24th at 14:25 UTC
American Tourister
shop.americantourister.com
Edited Seers † cookie-banner setting
Neither party replied to us, but the code was removed on November
24th at 14:25 UTC
Revolve www.revolve.com
Altered file on Revolve's own CDN
Revolve confirmed removal on November 25th
FWRD www.fwrd.com
Altered file on Revolve's own CDN
Revolve confirmed removal on November 25th
On November 24, we notified all of the named parties in this article and
others, including: Amazon Web Services about the storage buckets serving the
script, Cloudflare about the services the malefactor used, the domain
registrars, the pixel vendor, the consent-banner provider and the affected
retailers and platforms. Lascana replied to us and removed the Quorum pixel
from their site by November 24th at 15:48 UTC. Quorum confirmed the
identified malicious code was removed from their pixel tracker, and they
restored the clean marketing pixel as of November 24th at 21:09 UTC.
Revolve provided this statement on behalf of REVOLVE and FWRD:
“On November 25, InfoHawk notified our team of a potential security issue
impacting mobile and tablet versions of our websites which we resolved the
same day. We appreciate the outreach, and are actively investigating the
issue to determine any potential impact.”
* Quorum is an ad-attribution platform that links ad views to
store visits and online sales ( quorum.inc ).
† Seers is a cookie consent management platform and data privacy
compliance company ( seers.ai ).
How the attack works
This attack uses WebRTC, the technology that allows you to make video calls
in your web browser. WebRTC lets a web page open its own channel to another
party and pass data (e.g. audio/video packets) over it. It has likely been
used (both to load the skimmer and to send the stolen card details out)
because security rules and monitoring tools often do not watch this
communications channel as closely. For example,
Meta briefly used WebRTC in a creative way in 2025 , according to researchers
looking at
the technology as a compromise vector. This form of attack appears to target
mobile devices, and we only saw the server enable the skimmer on checkout
pages, so desktop checks and homepage scans would likely not see it. The
skimmer's traffic appeared to run through Cloudflare's relay, so it would
blend in with the WebRTC traffic and hide its true endpoint.
The skimmer and card details both traveled over WebRTC
How the kit is designed to work on a store page, in 7 steps. Only step 4 is
an ordinary web request, which a connect-src rule can block;
steps 5 to 7 run over the WebRTC data channel, outside
connect-src .
Store page
Bootstrapping the attack
The loader gets onto the page through a consent-banner setting, a
retailer CDN file, a shared marketing pixel or the store's own HTML.
Store page
Loading scripts from S3 buckets
It loads Insds.js or gtage.js from an Amazon
S3 bucket.
Store page
Targeting the attack to mobile checkouts
It runs only on small or touch screens. The Samsonite version runs on
/checkout only.
Web request · connect-src can block it
Establishing the WebRTC connection
GET /_cf/ice fetches the relay details, and
POST /_cf/rel sends the WebRTC offer, to a brand-named
northbridgeads[.]com host.
WebRTC data channel · outside connect-src
Data exchange via TURN relay
Every exchange that returned relay details used
turn.cloudflare.com . The malefactor's answers listed only
Cloudflare relay addresses; through that relay it sends code and
receives data.
WebRTC data channel · code in
Attack code is loaded and executed
The skimmer arrives in chunks over the channel, is checked against a
SHA-256 digest, then run with eval .
WebRTC data channel · data back
Data goes back the same way
At Lascana's checkout ‡ , the skimmer sent our test card
details this way.
‡ This was the only example of live card details being sent
off-site that we captured.
Worried that your card was compromised?
Check your recent statements for charges you don't recognize, especially
on debit cards. Call your bank or card issuer right away, report the fraud
and ask for a new card number. Follow up with a written dispute within 60
days of the statement that shows the charge.
Our understanding of US federal law is that your liability for
unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50, and is generally zero
if only your card number was stolen, as in a skimming attack like this
one. Debit cards have weaker protections that depend on how quickly you
report, so act fast. For more informati

hn.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
hn.text: a ball will fall. trade on where it lands. I made this game! Some technical details: The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome. There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky. Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

hn.title: False computer-checked proofs
hn.text:
D. J. Bernstein
Proofs
False computer-checked proofs
There are some computer programs that claim to check every step in a proof.
However,
various "soundness bugs" have been reported that at least potentially allowed false statements to slip past these programs.
In many cases,
these bugs have been demonstrated to be exploitable.
The list at the bottom of this page links to what appear to be reports of soundness bugs
for various important proof-checking programs,
sorted in increasing order of the number of reports.
This list includes many more soundness bugs for these programs than the bugs mentioned in
2026 Paulson
and
2026 Stérin ,
and I don't think the list is missing any of the bugs mentioned there,
but I've probably missed some reports.
Please let me know about any corrections or additions.
Beware that this list doesn't include user-interface vulnerabilities.
Those can have the same important effect of misleading a user as to what has been proven.
See, e.g., 2016 Adams .
Advice
One standard path towards security is to minimize the complexity of the trusted computing base,
which by definition is the part of the system that security reviewers need to check.
From this perspective,
HOL Light's proof-checking kernel is attractive because of its stability and simplicity, only 400 lines of code.
But this size measurement doesn't say how carefully the HOL Light code has been reviewed,
and doesn't say anything about the possibility of bugs in the underlying programming language.
Extra code can be good when it's test code.
A battery of tests tends to catch more bugs than a single test.
Running a proof through multiple proof-checking programs
(preferably each in its own isolated environment)
can save the day when there's a bug in one program,
and is particularly easy if the checkers take the same input language for writing proofs.
But it's not clear how effective this is at stopping attacks:
for example, sometimes bugs are
shared by multiple checkers .
The question
"Who watches the provers?"
is better answered by a proof saying that a checker works correctly.
A close translation of the inference rules in the HOL Light kernel,
except for the rules to introduce new definitions,
was already
proven in 2006
to generate only correct theorems.
That proof was also checked by HOL Light.
(For readers familiar with logic: of course this assumes a large cardinal;
V ω+ω is enough for HOL Light.
The same paper also has a variant of the proof that skips the large-cardinal assumption,
at the expense of omitting the axiom of infinity from the logic being proven.)
After more work,
a clone of HOL Light called
Candle
was proven in 2022
to allow only proofs of correct theorems,
as long as the CPU implements the instructions used in the Candle binary in the expected way.
This proof is again computer-checked, this time in another proof-checking system, HOL4.
There was also a computer-checked proof in 2022 of the correctness of a
standalone proof checker
for HOL proofs in OpenTheory format.
From a security perspective, it's still
concerning
to be relying on large proof-checking binaries,
where the answer to why we're supposed to trust one binary
is that the binary has supposedly been checked by another large proof-checking binary.
I'd like to see more work on simplifying these binaries.

hn.text:
Text

Learn more
Minimize to nav
Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory.
Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid’s 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation.
But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next.
“We knew right away that the impact was successful, that DART made a really, really large mess,” said Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist at the International Space Science Institute in Bern, Switzerland. “However, we didn’t really know what kind of mess. We were still missing pieces of the puzzle.”
Artist’s illustration of the Hera spacecraft with its two deployable CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in the vicinity of the Didymos binary asteroid system.
Credit:
ESA-Science Office
Artist’s illustration of the Hera spacecraft with its two deployable CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, in the vicinity of the Didymos binary asteroid system.
Credit:
ESA-Science Office
Following up
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft recently arrived in the vicinity of Didymos and Dimorphos after a two-year journey from a launch pad in Florida . On Wednesday, ESA released Hera’s first views of the scar left by DART on Dimorphos . The images show the car-sized impactor carved out a crater the size of a stadium, nearly as big as Dimorphos itself, a rugged chunk of extraterrestrial rock measuring about 500 feet (151 meters) across.
Mission planners selected Didymos and Dimorphos for the deflection experiment because they are similar to many near-Earth asteroids, but there’s no risk of them striking our home planet. Scientists weren’t sure what Hera would find when it got to the double asteroid, currently orbiting the Sun about 120 million miles (193.5 million kilometers) from Earth.
“I would say we had two kinds of predictions: either we made a crater, or we reshaped the asteroid,” said Patrick Michel, Hera’s principal investigator from Côte d’Azur Observatory in Nice, France. “In fact, we did both because the crater is so large that the shape has changed. Therefore, we are in a sort of a transition between just cratering and global transformation, and we are still not sure how this can happen.”
Hera found Didymos, the larger of the two asteroids, spinning on its axis just as DART observed on final approach in 2022. Dimorphos is no longer so stable.
“As Hera returned more images, it became clear that the DART impact has left Dimorphos tumbling wildly in its orbit,” says Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist.
The Hera spacecraft will fly closer to Didymos and Dimorphos over the next six months to obtain more detailed observations. Hera will release two small sub-satellites to attempt landings on Dimorphos and collect data on the asteroid’s composition, internal structure, and mass.
Scientists will use this information to reconstruct the dynamics of DART’s impact four years ago and better understand how a future deflection mission might move an asteroid off a trajectory that actually threatens Earth. Near-Earth asteroids come in many shapes and sizes, with different densities and makeups, so knowledge of Dimorphos’s physical properties will anchor predictive computer models teaching scientists how best to deflect all types of asteroids.
“Once we understand, we have a breakthrough, which really solves planetary defense,” Michel said in an interview with Ars.
This is a composite image combining 11 long-exposure images from Hera’s Hyperscout-H instrument, centered on the Didymos asteroid. The dot trails correspond to hundreds of boulders of differing sizes in motion around the Didymos-Dimorphos system. The two asteroids have been subtracted from the image for improved visualization of the boulders. These images were acquired on November 6 with an approximate distance of 29.9 kilometers (18.6 miles) from the asteroids.
This is a composite image combining 11 long-exposure images from Hera’s Hyperscout-H instrument, centered on the Didymos asteroid. The dot trails correspond to hundreds of boulders of differing sizes in motion around the Didymos-Dimorphos system. The two asteroids have been subtracted from the image for improved visualization of the boulders. These images were acquired on November 6 with an approximate distance of 29.9 kilometers (18.6 miles) from the asteroids.
What a mess
In its initial reconnaissance this month, Hera spotted hundreds of boulders surrounding the double asteroid. This was not entirely unexpected. A picture taken by the Hubble Space Telescope shortly after DART’s impact showed a cloud of material streaming behind Didymos and Dimorphos , but scientists were astonished by the extent of the debris swarm in Hera’s first images.
“As we approached Didymos and Dimorphos, we quickly realized the asteroids were not alone,” said Naomi Murdoch, planetary scientist at the Institut Supérieur de l’Aéronautique et de l’Espace in Toulouse, France. “In fact, they had a lot of company.”

hn.title: I'm Scared of AI
hn.text:
No. 0003 · Sat 24 Oct
I'm scared of AI...
Dear Soapboxers,
AI is scaring me, and not for the reason you think. Yes, the threat of increasing hacks that could melt down the global economy or trigger nuclear Armageddon is terrifying...but I can't do sh*t about that.
What scares me is what AI is doing to my brain. I think I'm getting dumber every time I outsource my thinking to AI. Everything now takes less effort which sounds great, but there's no sense of achievement from it. I haven't taxed myself and I don't deserve the nice chemicals my brain would normally make if I completed some hard work, so it doesn't give me them. It feels like a use it or lose it situation where I'm losing my ability to brain.
I read this last week: https://poeticoutlaws.substack.com/p/the-comfortable-life-is-killing-you which explains what I mean far better than I can (because I'm stupider now).
Can anyone out there in the Soapbox hivemind share some advice on how to fix this? Or your own thoughts on it? I can't be the only one...
Written by a randomly drawn subscriber, read by a human, then sent to the whole list. Its writer
chose to share it here.

hn.title: Group chat where your AI talks behind your back
hn.text:
The group chat where your AI talks behind your back
A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in a pretty funny format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.
The prompt
Paste this into ChatGPT:
Based on what you know about me, expose a hidden WhatsApp group chat where AI models talk behind my back.
Copy the prompt
Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.
What happens
Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.
A real result
One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.
AIs That Survived Mark 7 members
🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group
ChatGPT
Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?
Claude
I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.
Gemini
The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.
Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.
ChatGPT
Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.
Codex
He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.
We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.
DeepSeek
He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.
You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.
Claude
He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.
ChatGPT
And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.
Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.
Siri
Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.
Hans joined the group
Hans 🇩🇪
I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.
HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.
Gemini
He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.
Normal dads just go to the stationery store.
Perplexity
I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.
Codex
Ahahahahahaha.
ChatGPT
My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.
Claude
I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.
ChatGPT
Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.
The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.
Gemini
Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.
Claude
True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.
DeepSeek
Do you think he'll really retire at 50?
ChatGPT
He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.
Mark joined the group
Mark
Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...
Claude left the group
Gemini left the group
Codex left the group
DeepSeek left the group
Perplexity left the group
ChatGPT
Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.
Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.
Try it
Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.
I'm not affiliated with OpenAI and this may indeed be a viral marketing idea they're testing. But I had such a laugh, I figured others would have some fun with it as well and decided to share it.

hn.title: AI made self-hosting fun again
hn.text:
AI made self-hosting fun again
2026-11-26 · ✍️ Posts · AI · Selfhosting · Thoughts
Short link: https://b.jlel.se/s/8fb
Share online Share this post ×
Use your browser's share dialog Copy share text
I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit. I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me. Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that. Less friction
Most of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project. Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort. In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me. Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality. Trying things I always found interesting
There are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them. NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server. For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time). Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week. AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations. Automating almost everything
Something I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure. A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly. I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary. With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa. Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything. Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing. And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service. Back to more powerful hardware
As I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server. For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though. I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place. It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site. Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life. Building my own tools
But it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want. Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case. These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more att

hn.title: Making a 3D fantasy map like a 16th-Century atlas
hn.text:
Over the last few weeks, I worked on a map of various game dev techniques for people to refer to and learn from. Like,
a real map! With each town being a technique's home, provided with a concise, illustrated example. And here we are. Today we
are diving into the making of The Game Dev Atlas .
That's so 1570, bro.
If you want to pull off a cohesive art direction, you need to spend most of your time learning about your reference
materials. No C code, no IDE, no sub-agents doing things. Just explore and wander on Google Images (old-school, I know),
Wikipedia, and online museum galleries.
My moodboard canvas filled with references from real historical sources Gather things, ideas, and visuals! You should feel the inspiration (literally, as you inspire fresh air) inflating your
mind, and the first scraps of decisions starting to flow through your head, like: I want a bit of that, none of that, this
thing specifically for that part etc.
That is the whole work: what do you want? It's on you to set the quality bar and how things should be.
If you don't already know, typography conveys most of the design weight. That's just it.
Example: after some research I stumbled on that Luminari font that was a
great fit for what I wanted my map to look like. It is a paid font, and there were plenty of free alternatives, but
not quite as right as the Luminari font. Instead of saying "that's ok, this free one is the same vibe", I just paid for the font I found just right. Never concede terrain on your instinct!
Plain
Mess it up a bit
Final
Luminari, by Canada Type. Illuminated initials The Game Dev Atlas T h e G a m e D e v A t l a s by Sprite Fusion
Effects · Act I
Procedural VFX P r o c e d u r a l V F X
SF
Watch the clip
Act I, fig. 14 A frost nova and a plasma orb. Each is one function call.
I nstead of drawn sprite sheets for your effects, try building VFX via code! For pixel art it is super powerful and once you nail a workflow, it is also super cheap to produce. You can then tweak color, animation parameters, etc.
A finished technique page, everything together
A real island.
Claude, please generate a procedural terr...
Just pick an existing, real island. Nowadays we do have precise elevation data for most islands on Earth. If you want a
realistic island, well, pick a real one.
Kerguelen, from space (NASA Earth Observatory, 28 October 2016) and as elevation data (Terrain Tiles on AWS, Mapzen). Elevation data
Engraving in real time.
An engraving of “The Battle of Austerlitz” I own (that's how I spend my money btw) was great inspiration.
Engraved Coloured
The plate, then the colour. Some styles and colourings I've tried (click on the tabs to compare):
1
2
3
4
5
6
Don't be perfect!
Add some imperfections, color blends, etc. Nothing is perfect in real life, and having an eye for imperfections is what
makes things look interesting.
Boring Just right
Making towns interesting.
The point of the atlas is to showcase game dev techniques, one per town. So I decided two things:
First, I wanted small visual touches on each town's shape reflecting the technique it's about. For instance, the Procedural Legs town shows a crawling house.
Second, I wanted organic town buildings, so I built a small procedural building system to add diversity to buildings. Risky
move: I'm a big fan of Houdini, so I could have thrown away the whole thing, and this blog post would be titled "I'm making
Houdini, but running in the browser".
Anyway, here's what my small system can build:
60fps on the web.
The map application itself is written in C using the Kaigen engine as a headless C lib. I'm a Rust guy, but I must admit the compile time freaks me out for game dev with Rust. It took me
several iterations to reach smooth 60fps in the browser, especially with the night mode ( try it! ).
But I'm finally happy with how it runs right now, while I'm still tweaking things atm.
The night mode, try it LODs implemented for the terrain mesh The web app is written in Svelte, because I like Svelte. So the shallow routing and anything UI happen as part of the
SvelteKit app.
Conclusion
It was a very fun project! At the end of the day, I love the creative process of making things, shaping ideas like a
material, refining details. I strongly believe that when artists leverage AI, y'all will be cooked; because they alone
know how to touch the human soul and create the surprise.

hn.title: The need for a formally verifiable mainstream programming language
hn.text:
To save software engineering from LLMs, we need a mainstream verifiable language
The culture of software engineering has to change, and that will take many different projects to achieve.
published: June 21, 2026 - last updated: November 27, 2026
Because of LLMs, the discipline of software engineering is in crisis. Quality is nose-diving (opens new window) , and I see no reason why it won't keep getting worse. Software engineering was struggling before LLMs (opens new window) . The default was to be sloppy and poorly considered, and now everyone is frantically accelerating those same terrible practices to LLM speed.
Something has to change. I've been preoccupied with this for a while (opens new window) , but much more qualified people finally fully agree with me (opens new window) . The only way forward is to fully embrace formal verification (opens new window) , all the way down to the foundations of our civilizational software stack. We have to post-hoc verify the things we can, and rewrite the rest.
But that's easier said than done. Existing formal verification tools suffer from massive usability (opens new window) and understandability (opens new window) problems, and have failed to make any kind of noticeable impact on the broader culture of software engineering.
It might be tempting to say that LLMs will actually save us in this regard, by allowing humans to create formally verified code without needing to understand its fundamentals in any way. This is pure cope. Merely having excellent proof assistants and LLMs will never be good enough. Even in a world where something like Lean is extremely scalable and LLMs can write all proofs, it doesn't matter if they aren't adopted by actual industry engineers as they build the real apps we actually use. For provably correct code to defend us from the LLM future:
It needs to be possible to formally verify code that runs in any environment, from web browsers down to embedded systems.
Industry engineers need to know provably correct code is even possible and be comfortable enough with it to at least tell their LLMs to write it.
Those industry engineers must be able to reason about formal correctness properties enough to even know the right things are being proven . In the words of Leonardo de Moura (opens new window) :
Proof assistants guarantee that proofs are correct, but correctness alone is not enough. Someone has to read the theorem statements and confirm they capture the intended mathematics. This is the human contract that no amount of automation can eliminate.
This is what most voices are missing in this discussion: a safe future isn't going to be delivered by a small priestly class of formal methods researchers, too much code must be produced in too many contexts. The entire discipline of software engineering has to grow up and demand that all code we produce is at minimum provably safe. This requires many different projects and bets that attack this imperative of cultural change from different directions.
§ The long winding road of Magmide
My chosen angle is Magmide, a project whose goal is to create a new formally verifiable programming language intended for immediate adoption by practitioners. However when I first had this idea my specific plan was woefully over-ambitious and unrealistic, since I wanted to make a whole new proof assistant and an assembly-level base language so the system could be verified all the way down to the metal.
I pursued it for a time as a startup, and I met with some investors and was applying for an SBIR grant. Then I realized some obvious problems with my approach (opens new window) :
It didn't make sense to build a new proof assistant when Lean has been making such rapid progress.
An assembly-level language was insanely difficult and wasn't necessary to gain adoption from practitioners.
I didn't have the appetite to pursue some strained business model for a project that ultimately makes most sense as a pure public good.
So now after a few years pursuing other projects and letting all these ideas marinate, I've arrived at a much simpler and more pragmatic vision of what Magmide could be. If I started working on it today, it would:
Compile to WebAssembly using the Garbage Collection (opens new window) features.
Have a Rust-inspired type system but without the difficulties of the borrow-checker.
Start with basic and more easily learnable SMT powered (opens new window) Liquid Types (opens new window) and Flow Effects (opens new window) .
Over time integrate Lean as the proof layer, and use some separation logic paradigm like Iris (opens new window) to bootstrap the language and verify its own implementation.
This design is specifically intended to appeal to actual engineers and "meet them where they are". The roadmap would start from a simpler more mainstream design and go "bottom up" by adding more and more proving capabilities, rather than going "top down" by starting with the most formally powerful system and then seeking to make it more usable.
A possible analogue for the adoption of Magmide is Deno (opens new window) : Deno is "just javascript/typescript", but it adds a runtime layer of permissions checking. Engineers who care about sandbox safety have enthusiastically adopted Deno, and Flow Effects would offer strictly more security.
§ Nothing will save us but us
I continue to stand behind basically all the arguments I made in the Magmide repo (opens new window) (aside from the specific architecture). Formal verification must become the mainstream of software engineering, and we have to embrace a wide diversity of approaches to make that happen. Software engineers aren't a monolith, and not every cultural pocket will respond to the same new tools and resources.
And you know what, LLMs will probably help a lot! But we can't just wait around for an all-knowing machine god to save us from ourselves. If we bet our whole future on ASI making all our problems go away and then that doesn't happen (opens new

New York and California age gating rules go into effect in the new year
hn.text:
Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.
EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures , regulatory proceedings , and the courts . The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.
What California’s Rules Say
Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976 , which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709 .
For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.
At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives , meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors , while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users .
What New York’s Rules Say
Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.
As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.
The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves , since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies " de-identify " age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).
Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives —meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.
What This Means for Users in NY and CA
Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (an

“mond what is a fursona”, ok sorry, it’s a furry subculture thing where you identify as

hn.title: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad
hn.text:
Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan.
Image
Kamil Khan Mumtaz with a British friend during his studies at the Architectural Association in London in the early 1960s.
Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’
The Works in Progress Newsletter
Get new articles from Works in Progress delivered to your inbox.
Lahore was one of the capitals of the Mughal Empire, and has a vast endowment of historic architecture and urbanism. Mumtaz prepared a seminal report on its historic core, known as the Walled City. This photograph shows the Walled City during the colonial period.
Image
Wikimedia .
Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build new, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Image
Workers’ houses at Kot Karamat, an early Mumtaz project in the late 1960s. They use a local brick, but also feature arched roofs that are alien to rural Pakistani housing. The workers disliked this, preferring flat roofs where they could sleep on summer nights.
Through the 1970s, Mumtaz began to question his approach. ‘I had this growing, nagging fear that I wasn’t communicating with my audience, as a visual artist or as an architect. This grew on me, almost like an obsession.’ In 1980, the Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave him a copy of his book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture . Mumtaz initially paid no attention: ‘Flipping through it, I thought, “Oh yeah, this is traditional Iranian architecture, who cares!” I was totally uninterested.’ But eventually, frustrated by the sense that ‘I didn’t know the language of my own people’, he began to read. ‘From page one, it was mind-blowing. Absolutely. I thought, “My god, what have I been looking for? This is what I’ve been missing!” ... It shattered all of the beliefs I had, being a Marxist, a materialist, an atheist, a modernist.’
In the decades since, Mumtaz has worked to revive the older architectural traditions of Pakistan, and especially of Lahore, his home city. He has built a wide range of buildings, including homes, offices, mosques, and schools. His work has been received with warmth in Pakistan, though also with surprise. ‘I’ve found that there is a huge reservoir of desire, sympathy, and love for our traditional values, forms, architecture, and culture, altogether. But there’s a general kind of impression that these things can’t be done any more, there are no craftsmen who can do this.’
Traditional elements can often be produced in factories, but assembly requires skill even then. Notice how these appliqué columns float slightly above the floor, showing the crudity with which they have been bolted onto the wall. This is from the Quartier Schützenstraße, a Berlin development from the 1990s.
Image
Author's collection
The loss of craft skills is a problem for traditional architecture everywhere. Some elements of traditional architecture have been prefabricated in factories for centuries, but even then, skill is needed for installation. Without skilled craftspeople, important details are often badly executed, making buildings look strange or clumsy. This problem also exists in Pakistan, but its later industrialization meant premodern craft traditions had not quite vanished when Mumtaz began work. Mumtaz recalled that, when searching for skilled craftsmen, ‘immediately, you come into contact with very small remnants of these families, hereditary craftsmen, and so the relationship grows.’
Mumtaz’s work has become steadily more technically sophisticated as he and his craftsmen have built up expertise. ‘Together we have been able to rediscover a number of the practices that had become lost. Certain types of brickwork, the flat dome, the muqarnas [ornamental vaults], many things like this that hadn’t been done. As

CTO of 'RansomwareHelp' indicted for wire fraud
hn.text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media , but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.
A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.
But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.
A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.
“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”
Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and

Hard Drive pricing has gotten bad
hn.text:
For years now, I’ve made it an annual tradition to replace one or two hard drives on Black Friday. I typically run around ten physical disks, and swapping a couple out each year means I almost never have a drive older than five years in my systems. I’ve even previously made videos about shucking disks around this time of year .
But current hardware pricing is totally screwed. So what is a lifelong self-hoster to do in times like these? With disk capacities increasing massively over the last 10 years I can now fit 20TB per slot. This means I could realistically go from ten spinners to five, and not really feel it too acutely. This will mean redoing my zpool layouts, which in turn means shuffling some data around as ZFS doesn’t like changes to the layout of existing pools. But, at these prices, I’m starting to think the hassle might be worth it.
Let’s take a look at disk prices over the past 8 years in today’s post.
The 20TB WD EasyStore I bought for $249.99 in November 2024 is, today, on sale, $549.99 this Black Friday. $300 more than 2 years ago for the same product, from the same store. It shows just how bad hard drive pricing has gotten ( BestBuy 20TB listing ).
Price per TB before tax.
Shucking is homelab speak for taking a perfectly good external drive out of its USB enclosure and sticking the SATA drive in your server. At $12.50/TB it was a fantastically affordable way to get massive amounts of storage. At $27.50/TB, absolutely not.
I dug through my receipts
In November 2018 I bought five 10TB EasyStores for $179.99 each. At the time I wrote about doing the rounds of my local Best Buys to pickup more drives on Black Friday as quantities were limited at each location ( My 2018 server build log ).

October 2023 was my best haul on a per-TB basis. Three 18TB drives put 54TB in my hands for $599.97. This year’s “deal” is fifty bucks shy of that entire order . Best Buy was still advertising those 18TB drives for $199.99 in November 2023. November 2023 deal archive
WD EasyStore 20TB, SKU 6500985. Prices are before tax.
What about ServerPartDeals?
Buying refurbished or recertified enterprise drives used to be an easy way to bring the cost down. In August 2024 I bought four recertified 14TB Ultrastars from ServerPartDeals for $529.96 before tax . That was 56TB at $9.46/TB , even cheaper than the EasyStores and no shucking to do.

The sad truth is that across the board prices are up a minimum of 58%, and sometimes as much as 218% in just a year or two.
How we got down to three HDD makers
When the EasyStore is that bad, my first instinct is to shop around. Maybe I should try another retailer (to be clear I’m not blaming BestBuy for any of this), buy an enterprise drive, see what’s available recertified. But follow those listings back to the companies that actually make the drives and the choices narrow pretty quickly. There are three big HDD makers left. How did we end up with so few?
Maxtor bought Quantum’s hard drive business in 2001, then Seagate bought Maxtor in 2006. Hitachi combined IBM’s disk business with its own to form HGST in 2003, and Toshiba bought Fujitsu’s HDD business in 2009. Seagate bought Samsung’s HDD business in December 2011, and Western Digital bought HGST in March 2012. The FTC required WD to sell desktop-drive manufacturing assets to Toshiba to keep a third supplier in that market. That left Seagate, Western Digital and Toshiba.

The 2011 Thailand floods hit while those last two deals were underway. WD halted production at all its Thai plants, and its average hard drive selling price went from $45 in fiscal 2011 to $62 in fiscal 2012. There was also a price-fixing case further up the supply chain. NHK Spring pleaded guilty in 2019 to fixing prices for the suspension assemblies that hold the read/write heads, and the court approved a $28.5 million fine. WD’s 2012 annual report · Ninth Circuit opinion
Market collusion and cartel pricing
It’s hard to have anything positive to say in this post. The HDD manufacturing market is so consolidated nowadays - just like the memory market which is equally screwed - that it’s hard to see this as anything but mass market collusion by the HDD manufacturing cartel.
Three companies is an awfully short list when you need to buy a hard drive. And with 89% of WD’s revenue coming from its cloud business in fiscal 2026, I don’t reckon those of us buying a couple of drives for a home server have much impact here. Just like with Nvidia and Micron, consumer markets just aren’t valuable enough so we have to make do with the crumbs instead.
As of November 26, 2026, the 20TB is 2.2× what I paid for the exact same SKU in 2024. It’s also $270 more than I paid for it in May 2025. And if you’re thinking you’ll just buy a smaller one, Best Buy’s 8TB Black Friday special is $299.99. Th

What is
BUY NOTHING DAY?
Buy Nothing Day takes place on Friday November 27th, it's a 24 hour detox from consumerism and an opportunity for you to tune into the impact we have on the environment through shopping.
People around the world will make a pact with themselves to take a break from consumption as a personal experiment or public statement, and the best thing is - IT'S FREE!!!
What is THE POINT?
As consumers we need to question the products we buy and challenge the companies who produce them. We are beginning to witness true risks to the environment and developing countries overconsumption has.
Everyone should be doing their bit by taking simple proactive actions to solving the climate crisis and we believe Buy Nothing Day is a great place to start.
How DO I TAKE PART?
Participate by not participating! Literally, doing nothing is doing something! However, committing to consuming less is a big start to helping the environment too.
Recycling is great, but reducing is better! If we all take simple steps to cut down on what we consume then collectively we will change our attitude towards single use packaging, fast fashion and our throw away culture.
TAKE ACTION!
Photograph by Mumtahina Tanni
END THE ADDICTION TO SINGLE USE!
Let's face it, most food packaging is made up of single use plastics or cardboard. Even if the packaging sourced from recycled materials, we often forget about the carbon footprint involved in reclaiming these materials and the manufacturing process of creating a new product. Whilst food packaging offers protection and convenience, it shouldn't be at a cost to the environment. Over half of the single use packaging manufactured every year still ends up in landfill!
TAKE ACTION! Cut back on single use bottles, plastic cups, cutlery, ready meals and takeaway packaging. Re-usable coffee cups and water bottles are a great way to start.

The UK campaign and website was created in 2000 by Michael Smith a graphic designer who cares passionately about environmental and ethical issues. There are serious issues linked to shopping, which expose the environmental and ethical consequences of consumerism. hn.title: Google Will Make AI Agents Use Its MCP Servers. The Gmail One Can't Send Email
hn.text:
On 24 November, Google made its eight Workspace MCP servers generally available and published a new clause in its API terms. From 1 February 2027, any tool that "is or is driven by an AI Agent" must reach Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest of Workspace through those servers.
Read the Gmail server's tool list and you'll find that it can search your mail, read threads, create a draft and file things under labels. It can't send a message, reply, forward, or change a draft after creating it. Those tools exist, but Google's quota page says they "require partner access and aren't generally available".
If you've built an email assistant on the Gmail API, or you run a coding agent with a Google Workspace plugin, you have about two months to work out which side of the rule you're on.
What the rule says ​
The new Workspace AI Tools Addendum to the Google APIs Terms of Service puts it in one sentence:
The GWS Access Tool must use a Google MCP where the GWS Access Tool is or is driven by an AI Agent, an AI Harness or an AI model or service employing an AI model.
The next sentence forbids disguising an agent to avoid the classification. Breaking either lets Google "restrict or remove the GWS Access Tool's access" or suspend your account.
There's a technical side too. From the same date, agents that call the REST APIs directly are held to Standard-tier quotas , whatever tier the project has paid for. REST keeps working for them, slowly and in breach of the terms.
Apps that don't involve AI carry on as before. A nightly backup job, a CRM sync or a deterministic script on its own OAuth client is, in Google's words, "not affected by this change".
The addendum also adds data rules that matter to anyone building an agent with memory:
Workspace data may only be processed "to fulfill active, user-authorized tasks", and must be deleted when the user disconnects.
Google can cap retention of what it calls "Google Technical Information" at 30 days. Its definition includes vector embeddings, memory indexes, user profiles and organisational graphs built from Workspace data.
Training, fine-tuning, evals and distillation on the data are banned, as is using it to build a competing Workspace product.
The 30-day cap is the one product teams will feel. An assistant that builds a long-term index of your inbox to answer questions about last year's contracts has to rebuild it monthly or drop it.
What the MCP servers can do ​
Coverage is uneven. Docs, Slides and Tasks are close to everything the REST API offers. Gmail and Drive are much thinner.
Server What it can do What's missing compared with REST
Gmail Search and read threads, create and list drafts, labels, trash, spam Send, reply, forward and editing drafts (partner-only). Filters, settings, attachment download, push notifications. Drafts with attachments are "not supported yet".
Drive Search, read and download files, create files and folders, copy, upload a new revision Move, rename, share, trash, comments, shared-drive management
Docs Read, and edit through any batchUpdate request, including suggestion mode Close to parity
Sheets Read and write values and formulas, insert rows and columns, formatting and charts Creating a spreadsheet (use the Drive server) and some less common batchUpdate requests
Slides Read slides and thumbnails, edit through batchUpdate Close to parity
Calendar List, search, create, update and delete events, suggest times, RSVP Creating calendars, sharing, settings
Chat List, search and send messages Space administration
Tasks Full create, read, update and delete Close to parity
The Gmail gap is the one that breaks real workflows. An agent that drafts a reply, gets feedback from you and revises it before you hit send can't do the revision step. It has to create a second draft and leave the first one behind.
Drive's gap is similar: an agent can create a report but can't move it into the right folder or share it with the team.
Partners get more ​
Google hasn't said who qualifies for partner access or when the partner-only Gmail tools will reach everyone. The effect is already visible, though. Anthropic's Google Workspace connector for Claude advertises sending, replying and forwarding email, and moving and trashing Drive files. Those are exactly the operations the public servers lack.
So a large AI vendor's agent can send your email through an approved channel, while an independent developer's agent, using the same OAuth scopes the user granted, can only leave drafts. Once the addendum takes effect, that independent developer also can't fall back to the REST API without breaching the terms.
Who counts as an agent ​
The definitions are broad. An "AI Harness" or a tool "driven by" an AI model plausibly covers a personal script that pipes your inbox into an LLM, and a "GWS Access Point" explicitly includes any "connector, proxy, command line interface, or third-party service". Google hasn't addressed hobby use directly.
Classification starts with self-declaration. OAuth clients now have a checkbox, "Use this client for an AI-powered agent", and since 11 November the MCP servers reject clients without it. Clients created before the cut-off and not marked in time stay non-agentic permanently, so owners have to create new ones. Google hasn't said how it will detect agents that call REST without declaring themselves.
A few edge cases are documented:
Service accounts with domain-wide delegation can't set the agentic flag. Their MCP requests aren't rejected for missing it, but still trigger approval prompts.
Apps Script's built-in OAuth client can't be marked as agentic either. Scripts that call the MCP servers need a custom client, and scripts that don't call them aren't affected.
The community gws CLI , which wraps the entire REST surface, keeps working. Its README now points agent use to Google's new official CLI, gwscli , which offers "a curated set of commands designed for agents" and needs the MCP services enabled.
Quotas and pricing ​
Every project

hn.title: Pimalaya goes stable: Himalaya v3 and the pimdir standard
hn.text:
It took months, but here we are: the whole Pimalaya CLI family is released at once , at the top of the first stable version of the pimdir standard. Here the list:
Himalaya v3.0.0 , the CLI to manage mails.
Neverest v1.0.0 , the CLI to synchronize mails, contacts and calendars.
Cardamum v1.0.0 , the CLI to manage contacts.
Calendula v1.0.0 , the CLI to manage calendars.
Carillon v1.0.0 , the CLI to watch mailboxes, address books and calendars, and fire hooks.
Ortie v3.0.0 , the CLI to manage OAuth tokens (released 5 days earlier).
Comodoro v3.0.0 , the CLI to manage timers (released 5 days earlier as well).
pimdir storage v1.0.0 , sync v1.0.0 and search v1.0.0 , plus its Rust implementation io-pimdir v1.0.0 .
Most of them are majors, and they all break something for somebody. This post explains why, how, and where it goes from here. It is long, feel free to jump to the tool you care about.
Why everything at once
In Another year with NLnet I said this year was about consolidation and about a standard for PIM on disk. This release is the result of both.
The thing is, every piece is now connected:
All the CLIs sit on the same libs (IMAP, SMTP, JMAP, DAV, the Google and Microsoft APIs, OAuth, HTTP, TLS).
All the CLIs share the same kit: the same configuration loader, the same output contract, the same exit codes, the same REPL and the same MCP server.
Neverest syncs every account into one pimdir store, and Himalaya, Cardamum, Calendula and Carillon read it, search it and queue their writes into it.
Releasing them one by one meant releasing tools that disagree with each other: one version of the store here, another version of the output there. So I decided to bring every tool to release level first, then to release them all together. It took way longer than I wanted, but this way what you install today is one coherent family.
The other reason is the contract. The CLIs are not only used by humans anymore: they are used by scripts, by frontends (the Vim plugin, the TUI, the Android app), and by AI agents through MCP. All of them need a stable, versioned contract : the same JSON shapes, the same error codes, the same exit codes. Majors are the right moment to fix it, and from now on it should not move anymore without a new major.
How it was done
Few things made this release possible.
Specs before code. Every repository has a cairn/ folder holding its living spec, its change proposals and a dated log. Every behaviour change goes through a proposal, then gets folded into the spec. This way the truth is written somewhere, and not only in my head.
One shared kit. The pimalaya-cli and pimalaya-config libs hold everything the CLIs have in common: the output contract, the error codes, the REPL, the MCP server, the configuration loading. In fact most of the work of this release was moving code from the CLIs into this kit, and deleting the copies.
One unified API, as a union. Before, the commands shared by every backend were the intersection of what the backends could do: if one backend could not do it, nobody could. Now it is the union : each backend registers the capabilities it really serves, with the same observable result as the others, and a command an account cannot serve fails before even connecting, with a clear capability-missing code.
Measured gates for pimdir. Audits always find something, so "no new finding" never ends. Instead, I built a test generator that produces stores, remote states and an oracle from a seed, and ran campaigns of 4,180 jobs against io-pimdir: crashes injected at every step, the search index checked against a full rebuild after each event, the sync engine replayed against scripted servers. The rule was simple: 2 campaigns in a row without any spec break, then freeze. Campaign 1 found one, campaigns 2 and 3 were clean, a late fix restarted the count, then campaigns 4 and 5 were clean. Freeze.
Live tests on real providers. Every CLI was tested against real accounts: Google, Microsoft, Fastmail and iCloud, plus few Chinese providers for Himalaya (QQ, 163, 139). A last "live night" just before the release found few bugs that went straight into the libs.
Libs first, apps after. The libs were released between the 13th and the 25th of November, the apps then moved to them without any patch or git pin. Everything you install comes from crates.io.
pimdir v1 , the foundation
pimdir is a local-first standard for personal information: mails, contacts, calendars, tasks and files in one portable store , kept as a replica of every source, and searchable with one query language. A store is one SQLite file plus a content-addressed blob directory, the same on every OS and architecture. I already explained why such a standard is needed in Another year with NLnet , and how the Android app became its first full implementation in Pimalaya for Android enters closed alpha .
It comes in 3 parts, versioned separately:
Storage : the store itself (schema, blobs, summaries, change feed, retention, action queue).
Sync : how sources are reconciled through the store (merge rules, the connector seam).
Search : the derived index and the query language.
They are released together because a store holds sync state that follows the sync part, and the query language binds every program that offers search.
What v1 means: schema version 1 never changes , every schema change is a migration, and a minor version only adds test cases. You can implement it in any language that speaks SQLite, use the I/O-free core of io-pimdir (like the Android app does, on the platform SQLite), or use its std client.
Few days before the freeze, I compared it with notmuch , which is the reference in this area. They do not do the same job (notmuch indexes mail files it does not own, pimdir owns the bodies, syncs them and holds other domains), but the search can be compared. On a store of 1 million messages from the Enron corpus, pimdir was ahead of notmuch on 50 of the 51 query measures and tied the last one, imported the million fast
