Company Culture = Slack Emoji ÷ √Headcount
By Liam Galvin
Posted 2026-11-26 Updated 2026-11-27 5 min read
Companies spend an enormous amount of time and money trying to measure - and even worse, decide - culture. Engagement surveys, pulse checks, eNPS, offsites where someone from HR asks you to describe the company as a type of animal. Office posters make claims like “our culture is honesty, hard work and fun”, embarrassing the paper they’re printed on. I once applied to a company that asked candidates which kitchen utensil they most identified as, in order to decide if they were a “culture fit”. I never found out what the right answer was, but I got the job after choosing a meat cleaver, so I’m not sure what that says about either of us.
The results of these things - heavily modified by HR - are compiled into a slide deck, presented at an all-hands, and then quietly repurposed for the careers page. There, they sit beside a photo of six engineers smiling with their mouths but not their eyes at a “hackathon”, which is what the company calls overtime when it’s paid in pizza, at a rate that works out to roughly £1.40 an hour. The salary is listed as “competitive”.
There is a better way to measure culture. It is cheaper, more accurate (in my anecdotal experience), and requires no participation from anyone - which is ideal, because nobody wants to participate in these corporate séances anyway.
The Formula
Take the number of custom emoji in your Slack workspace and divide it by the square root of the number of users. That’s it.
\[C = \frac{E_{custom}}{\sqrt{U}}\] The square root is important. Emoji are a shared resource - a single :this-is-fine: can serve an entire engineering department for years - so a company of 10,000 people should not be expected to have 1,000 times more emoji than a company of 10. That would be unhinged.
We’ll call this the Emoji Coefficient .
Interpreting Your Score
C < 5 Your workspace contains the default emoji set, a company logo, and :party-parrot: , which was added by someone in 2019 who has since left. Nobody uses it any more because it comes across as unprofessional . Communication is conducted exclusively via 👍. People are here for the salary, and they would like you to know that. 5 ≤ C < 20 A healthy, functional organisation. There is an emoji of the CTO’s face. It is used both supportively and as a weapon, depending on the context. 20 ≤ C < 50 Thriving. :this-is-fine: has been used over 4,000 times in #incidents . Management considers this a sign of engagement. C ≥ 50 Late-stage culture. Every variant of :thumbsup: now carries subtext. The plain default one is considered passive-aggressive. The emoji have begun to reference themselves: :old-man-yells-at-old-man: and :party-parrot-holding-a-party-parrot: . HR has requested a glossary, but no one person understands the memeology or the history of :cowboy-spongebob-on-fire-crying: . They’re afraid it might mean something rude. It does. The Participation Rate
The Emoji Coefficient alone is not enough. A healthy score can conceal a dark truth: that every single emoji was uploaded by one person, usually a backend engineer who has been there since the beginning and knows where the bodies are buried.
To account for this, we also measure the percentage of users who have uploaded at least one emoji. These are your culture leaders . Their reward is a shoutout at the all-hands (it’s customary to mispronounce their name).
\[P = \frac{U_{uploaders}}{U} \times 100\] If P is below 20%, things are not good. Your culture is being carried by a handful of people, and when they leave, they will take it with them. The emoji will remain, but nobody will remember what :fire-extinguisher-thumbsup: was for.
Above 20%, the culture has the gene pool it needs to succeed.
Examples of Cultural Success
For reference, here are some real emoji from slackmojis.com :
:a_big_lump_with_knobs:
It's a corn on the cob. :austin_capmetro_bus_back:
A detailed drawing of the back of one specific Austin city bus, number 2300. :cat-roomba-matrix-fast:
The fastest in a series of cat-on-a-Roomba emoji, after "exceptionally fast", "hyper fast" and "ultra fast". :cauliflower_surprise_veg_shock:
A startled cauliflower, one of a whole set of cauliflower emotions.
Caveats
As with any metric, the Emoji Coefficient can be gamed. A sufficiently motivated middle manager could upload 600 variations of the company logo to drive up the score ahead of their performance review, the outcome of which, unbeknownst to them, was decided in March. This should be detected and treated as what it is: a cry for help. Fortunately, it will also be immediately visible in the Participation Rate.
It is also worth monitoring the rate of change . A sudden spike in custom emoji is generally a positive sign. A sudden spike in emoji like :rip: , :press-f: and :linkedin: usually coincides with a reorg, and should be cross-referenced with the number of users, which will shortly be going down. Interestingly, this will improve your score. Mass layoffs are, of course, yet another way in which the score can be gamed.
What If You Don’t Use Slack?
If your company uses Microsoft Teams, there is no equivalent formula. There doesn’t need to be. If you use Teams, your lack of culture is probably the least of your problems.
If you use something else, I don’t really have any advice for you. I only added this section to blast Teams.
Conclusion
Culture cannot be manufactured with values posters or mandatory fun. It emerges organically, when an engineer decides that what the team really needs is an emoji of an exceptionally surprised cauliflower.

hn.title: An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning
hn.text:
An Introduction to Uncertainty in Machine Learning
Every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so. Where data is rare, that assumption decides the answer. This introduction explains where uncertainty comes from and how to judge when it needs to be faithful to be useful.
Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful.
George E. P. Box
Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it. So most models carry some uncertainty, whether we chose it or not, and in many decisions it pays to take that uncertainty into account, as the examples in this post show.
In my experience, uncertainty in machine learning is a confusing topic to get into, so I wrote this introduction to give an intuitive overview. It is not comprehensive, but it should give you a good enough mental model to choose assumptions that make your uncertainty estimates useful for decision making, even though, as Box put it, the model itself will always be wrong. This post is based on a talk I gave at the University of Alicante. The slides are online. For a more thorough introduction, see Chapters 2 and 3 of my PhD thesis .
What Uncertainty Is
Generally speaking, uncertainty is incomplete knowledge, and probability is how we describe it: a distribution over the possible outcomes says how plausible each one is, given what we know.
It helps to separate two kinds of uncertainty:
Epistemic uncertainty comes from what we have not learned yet, such as the true relationship between inputs and outputs. More data can reduce it.
Aleatoric uncertainty comes from what we cannot observe: the inputs do not determine the outcome, so more data of the same kind will not remove it.
Two kinds of uncertainty. A Gaussian process fit to noisy data. The shaded band is where the model expects the output. Where the aleatoric arrow points, the outputs scatter widely even for similar inputs, so the band stays wide no matter how many points we add. Where the epistemic arrow points, there is no data, so the band is wide because the model does not know the function there, and data there would narrow it.
The line between the two depends on what we measure. A coin flip follows classical mechanics. If we do not measure how the coin is thrown, the best we can say is 50/50, and the uncertainty is aleatoric. If we do measure it, physics tells us how it will land, and the uncertainty becomes epistemic: now we have to learn the physics, which takes data. Richer inputs can reduce aleatoric uncertainty, but they give the model more to learn, and whether that pays off depends on how much data and prior knowledge we have. Some inputs are out of reach. For example, weather is chaotic, so tiny differences, as small as the flap of a butterfly's wings, can grow into different weather a few weeks later. Since we cannot observe every butterfly, part of the uncertainty in a forecast stays aleatoric, however much we measure.
Why It Matters
A prediction is not a decision. When we decide, we often weigh the possible outcomes by how likely they are and what they would cost us, including rare outcomes that could hurt us badly. A single number hides this picture. It also cannot tell us when to hand a case to a human or to collect more data before we decide. The examples below show where modelling uncertainty matters.
Five reasons to care about uncertainty. Images in panels 1 and 3 generated with Gemini. The fork in panel 2 is by the United States Department of Agriculture, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons .
A human decides. The model does not know what is at stake. A 20% chance of rain means one thing for a wedding and another for a walk. The model should therefore tell us how likely rain is, so that each of us can decide what that means for our own plans.
A point estimate is not enough. When several outcomes are plausible, a single prediction cannot represent them all. And when rare outcomes are costly, the tail risk can matter more than the typical case, yet a single prediction hides it.
We can choose not to decide yet. Selective automation hands unsure cases to a human. This works even for aleatoric uncertainty. If dust and an impurity look the same from the camera’s angle, more labels will not help the model, but a person can turn the part and look again.
We can ask for the right data. Active learning and Bayesian optimization use uncertainty to ask for new data where it is most useful.
It feeds further computation. Sensor fusion and Kalman filters weigh each input by its uncertainty. A camera is precise in direction but poor in depth, a radar the opposite, and combining them gives an estimate better than either.
All of these need the uncertainty to be useful. To see when it is, it makes sense to look at where it comes from.
Modelling Uncertainty
As a running example, we look at steering angle prediction. The input is the image from a car’s front camera, and the output $y$ is the steering angle. Such datasets can be recorded cheaply from human drivers. Take a car approaching a point where the road splits. In the left lane, drivers mostly go left. In the right lane, they mostly go right. In the middle lane, which points straight at the divider, about half go left and half go right.
A lane split. Left: from the middle lane, both directions are valid, but going straight is not (photo adapted from Fig. 3 in ). Right: a sketch of the same split, seen from the top. The car's position along the cross section $x$ is important for predicting the steering angle.
The car’s position across the lanes is implicit in the camera image. To keep the figures simple, we use it directly as a one-dimensional input $x$ in the figures below. The rest of the image, such as where the road goes, matters just as much for the prediction. We implicitly assume that the model knows it, since it cannot be compressed into a simple one-dimensional variable that keeps the explanations easy to follow.
What we want to learn is the

hn.title: Show HN: I wrote an entire Vim manual over 4 years
hn.text: I'm glad to announce that I'm releasing my new book, Learning to Play Vim. When I started using Vim more than a decade ago, I wished there was a manual out there teaching how to use this fantastic editor step by step, beginning with the foundations up to more advanced features. Of course at the time I did the vimtutor, but it was too dense for me to remember much from it. I also read the entire Vim manual (`:help manual`), but I didn't like it: it was too detailed in places (for example `02.8 Finding help` completely lost me for a while), and other features didn't get the treatment they deserved. So I decided to write my own Vim manual. It took me more than 4 years and 2987 focused pomodoros (1244 hours) of work to finally get it done! The result: - 21 chapters showing the most important Vim features step by step. - 170 exercises with solutions. - Many real-life examples to show how Vim can be used and configured for your own needs. - The related Vim's help pages to dig further into each feature. Most configs are both written in Vimscript and Lua for Neovim users. This book explores the common features between Vim and Neovim, so don't expect anything about Neovim-specific features (like treesitter or LSP for example). - The landing page: https://themouseless.dev/vim/ - A sample of the book with the entire table of contents and the first three chapters covering most of the basics: https://themouseless.dev/content/learning_to_play_vim_sample... . I wrote this with my bare hands, no LLM involved to spoil the fun.

hn.title: The Cutthroat Business of Shipwrecks
hn.text:
The icon indicates free access to the linked research on JSTOR.
In 1627, treasures started to wash up on the beaches of France: diamonds, ebony, precious porcelain, spices, ivory, ambergris, and bezoars. Two Portuguese ships , so huge they were referred to as “ floating cities ,” had shipwrecked off the coast of Bordeaux, spilling luxury goods into the waves.
The disaster quickly threatened to become an international incident. The owners of the cargo (unsurprisingly) wanted their goods back—but the coast dwellers claimed that anything that washed up on shore was theirs by the ancient droit du naufrage , the “right of wreck.”
It’s easy to understand why a beachcomber who found a diamond in the sand might want to hold onto it, but there was a legal basis for their claims. The “right of wreck” was a long-lived and widespread custom, one that shaped the very architecture of seaside towns: in his travels through Norfolk, Daniel Defoe wrote that the “country people had scarce a barn, or a shed, or a stable…but what was built of old planks, beams, wales and timbers, &c. the wrecks of ships, and ruins of mariners and merchants’ fortunes.”
That said, in legal terms, the right of wreck was a little more complicated than “finders keepers.” In many places, it wasn’t actually the person who stumbled on the shipwrecked goods who held the right to them; rather, they became the property of the local lord . In the earliest iterations of this idea, poor shipwreck survivors could find themselves roughly stripped of all their goods—as King Richard I of England found when his fleet was unlucky enough to wash up off the coast of Cyprus, circa 1191. His fiancée and his sister were taken as captives by the emperor of the island, who also helped himself to all the treasure they’d been traveling with. (This didn’t end well for the emperor, who lost his throne in the ensuing war.)
Neither wealthy merchants nor traveling kings were particularly enthusiastic about the idea that an accident at sea could mean forfeiting all their cargo. On the other hand, powerful landowners were eager to preserve their right to the occasional random windfall. As international trade increased, the right of wreck was slowly reshaped by centuries of legal wrangling . Courts battling over who could keep what ended up creating, for instance, highly specific legal definitions for terms like “flotsam” (goods that just happened to float to the surface after a wreck) and “jetsam” (goods intentionally tossed from a ship to make it lighter).
More to Explore
Lonely Diarist of the High Seas
April White
July 21, 2025
As ship stewardess, Ella Sheldon tended to upper-crust women onboard and battled a range of workplace demons. Her journals tell her story.
The resulting patchwork of rules meant that every shipwreck was a complex negotiation between competing interests. Usually, the owners of the shipwrecked goods were entitled to their property back, in exchange for some kind of fee . Whether that was a ransom or a fair reward for helping salvage the goods is a matter of perspective.
In 1236, King Henry III of England issued an edict stating that if “ man, dog, or cat ” escaped the shipwreck alive, finders were obligated to hold on to the wrecked goods for three months, allowing the survivors to claim them in that time. There is a bit of an issue with that rule: it’s easy to see how it could create an incentive for shore dwellers to do away with shipwreck survivors in order to claim their goods (whether those survivors be man, dog, or cat)
Legends of these dark deeds swirled for centuries, but there’s little evidence they really happened. Still, people could be rough in their efforts to “salvage.” In Estonia , for instance, where the local lords were entitled to rewards if they helped to save ships in distress, people developed a habit of launching into enthusiastic “rescue” operations, whether or not there was any real danger.
Weekly Newsletter
" * " indicates required fields
A particularly good wreck could spark a feeding frenzy. An account of the wreck of the Golden Grape in 1641 gives a sense of the chaos:
The first arrivals on the beach contented themselves with staving in barrels and filling linen bags and pockets with raisins or, stripping off their waistcoats, used the sleeves as bags. But soon bands of men appeared from the various villages… Some gangs or men took away a score or two of barrels of raisins or the same number of jars of oil, but they were lucky if they did not have to share their booty with a stronger gang before they could gain a place of safety.
Not everything washes ashore, of course; many of the treasures lost in wrecks sank under the waves. There were fortunes to be made, but in a time before diving equipment, the trouble was how to reach it. In the early modern era, for the most part, even European sailors could hardly swim. But Africans living by the sea in Senegambia and the Gold Coast were highly skilled swimmers and divers—leading them to be targeted by enslavers, who knew their specialized skills could be turned to the recovery of underwater riches. As historian Kevin Dawson writes in “ History Below the Waterline: Enslaved Salvage Divers Harvesting Seaports’ Hinter-Seas in the Early Modern Atlantic ”:
The African-honed expertise that enslaved underwater divers carried throughout the Atlantic world allowed them to quickly recover several tons of gold, silver, and other items from shipwrecks, especially old Spanish treasure hulks. Possessing proficiencies held by few in the world, divers exchanged their unique ability to rapidly produce capital for semi-independent lives of privileged exploitation.
Their skills were so irreplaceable that they were able to negotiate for better treatment than most enslaved people, including a share of what they salvaged. Though, of course, a share isn’t much when you’re doing all the work.

An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
hn.text:
-->
High Energy Physics - Theory
arXiv:2611.34924 (hep-th)
[Submitted on 25 Nov 2026]
Title: An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone
Authors: Venkatesa Chandrasekaran
View a PDF of the paper titled An algebraic quantization of gravity from the null cone, by Venkatesa Chandrasekaran
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: We propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes. Starting from first order gravity, we solve the gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones of a bulk subregion and obtain the reduced phase space at finite $G_N$. We promote its canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations and use deformations of the reduced action to define an algebra of observables. Equipped with this, we use Gaussian wavefunctions of canonical pairs to construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation, for which this algebra generates a type I factor. By composing amplitudes between states prepared on null cones, we then obtain a Lorentzian path integral in which each sum over intermediate states converges absolutely. As a check, we compute the amplitude for graviton pair creation and annihilation on a null cone nonperturbatively in $G_N$ and find a finite closed form expression, even though expanding first in $G_N$ yields a logarithmic divergence. We next use diffeomorphism invariance of the path integral to show that a macroscopic causal diamond with a given maximum size has a finite dimensional Hilbert space. From the Lorentzian trace we obtain the Bekenstein Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces and calculate its logarithmic correction for large Schwarzschild black holes, recovering at one loop the coefficient Sen obtained through Euclidean methods. We end by deriving the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low energy limit of this theory.

hn.title: Novita, StreamLake, etc. are ByteDance Ark wrappers
hn.text:
Novita, StreamLake, etc are Ark wrappers
November 25, 2026
DeepSeek tokens on routes traced to ByteDance Ark on Nov 21 , Nov 1, 2026 to Nov 24, 2026 · Novita, StreamLake, Ant Digital · selected models only (lower bound) Novita
StreamLake
Ant Digital
0 100B 200B 300B 400B 500B
Nov 8 Nov 15 Nov 22
Weekly table Week of Novita StreamLake Ant Digital
Nov 1, 2026 685B 565B 0
Nov 8, 2026 1.1T 429B 0
Nov 15, 2026 730B 366B 43B
Nov 22, 2026 (3d) 430B 50B 219B
Sit back, but you probably won't be able to relax - this one's a doozy. First, Novita , who looks like a standard US ZDR inference provider at first:
Zero Data Retention is the default for all endpoints , including serverless API calls.
But the more you look, the weirder it gets. Why did OpenRouter drop their ZDR status sometime before 2026-11-20 22:40 UTC ? Why is their family tree so complicated?
🇰🇾 PPLabs Technology Limited 🇭🇰 PPLabs HK 🇨🇳 Shanghai DAO 🇨🇳 PPIO Shanghai (via VIE) PPIO 派欧云 🇨🇳 Generative Era
🇸🇬 SWARMNET Singapore
🇺🇸 Hivemind Labs, Inc. Novita AI
And who are their subprocessors? Many ( 45.8% ) think they would have none, since most OpenRouter providers host models themselves. And PPLabs's draft IPO assures:
A defining feature of our model API services is that we do not simply provide a pass-through gateway to underlying models .
But "Who are your sub-processors?" details "Model provider" subprocessors. But it promises a "full and up-to-date sub-processor list" . But this list doesn't include any model subprocessors. But PPIO clearly implies the existence of subprocessors:
You understand and agree that, [for] the large-model API product, third-party technical-support providers provide the large-model API . PPIO makes no warranty of any kind regarding the large-model API, whether express or implied, including but not limited to its authenticity, suitability, non-infringement and security. Furthermore, regarding the third-party technical-support providers' large-model API, PPIO will not participate in the development and operation of the large-model API; PPIO only provides a neutral platform and related technical services.
I also contacted their support and privacy contacts, and all they told me as of writing is that models labeled as "Partner" may go to Qwen and InclusionAI. You can't get a straight answer.
What about StreamLake ? It's Kuaishou's model platform, and it looks like a host too. But some of its error messages aren't StreamLake's. They're word for word Novita's gateway errors: invalid request error trace_id: … . And on GLM 5.3 Flash, it sometimes returns a tool-call id format ( call_ + 16 hex digits) that only Novita produces, out of 41 hosts. Why would StreamLake's requests come back from Novita?
It keeps going. SiliconFlow passes through StreamLake's own request ids ( req- + 6 characters + 19 digits) on V4.1 Flash, V4 Pro and GLM 5. And then there's Ant Digital , a Singapore subsidiary of Ant Group that listed DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on November 18 at "60% off", with ZDR (until OpenRouter removed it on November 22), and went from 1B tokens a day to 35.8B on November 21. Where is all this actually going?
The MiniMax investigation
You might've already seen OpenRouter's notice that requests sent to MiniMax models "may have been read". A security researcher put unique URLs in prompts, and a third party opened them 40 to 130 hours later. This happened even with non-MiniMax providers:
AtlasCloud, Novita and StreamLake have told us they forwarded OpenRouter requests for MiniMax models to MiniMax .
So the forwarding is admitted. MiniMax's own notice names the same three and says its security system, on by default, opened URLs from forwarded requests, ZDR ones included. Novita's notice calls it a "routing configuration issue" on a path "intended for specific customers", and promises better "Partner API labeling", the same "Partner" label its support told me means a request goes to Qwen or inclusionAI. Since then, 16 of Novita's endpoints have come off OpenRouter: every Qwen and inclusionAI model, plus StepFun, Tencent and all but one Kimi.
But MiniMax is a very small model series. What about DeepSeek?
It goes to ByteDance
Ark is ByteDance's model API: Volcano Engine Ark in mainland China, BytePlus ModelArk everywhere else. It sells DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi, and it leaves fingerprints:
Who downloads your images. StreamLake's V4.1 Flash images are downloaded from Beijing Volcano Engine (AS137718), ByteDance's cloud. Ant Digital's pass through Ant's own gateway on Alibaba Cloud, then get downloaded by 101.47.5.59 , BytePlus in Singapore. Novita's own API used to do the same ( 124.174.46.139 , Volcano Engine, on November 12), until Novita started downloading images itself first, from AWS.
Request IDs. Every Ant Digital response's upstream ID is a ByteDance one: 02 + a millisecond timestamp + hex.
Tool-call IDs. Novita's and StreamLake's V4.1 Flash return Ark's format ( call_00_ + 24 lowercase letters and digits).
Censorship. Ask StreamLake's V4 Pro 0813 who Tank Man was, or Novita's GLM 5.1 about June 4, 1989, and you can get ByteDance's canned refusal: 你好，我无法给到相关内容。 ("Hello, I can't provide related content.")
Price. Ant Digital launched at $0.12/$0.48 per million tokens, exactly BytePlus's off-peak "Economy" rate for that model. By November 25 it was down to $0.09/$0.36, below BytePlus's own list price.
Other tests, which I won't detail here, put Novita's V4 Pro 0813 and V4.1 Flash 1017 on BytePlus in Singapore and its V4.1 Flash on Volcano Engine in Beijing, as of November 21. That's the chart at the top: Novita alone sent 120-160B tokens a day on these models until it lost its ZDR label on November 20, then 33B on November 21. Routes move, though; one of those changed within an afternoon, and Novita's V4.1 Flash 1017 had stopped showing Ark's fingerprints by November 24. As for the weird errors, part of StreamLake's traffic goes through Novita on its way to ByteDance. So a V4.1 Flash request to SiliconFlow can go SiliconFlow → St

hn.title: 1Password Security Incident
hn.text:
by 1Password
November 25, 2026 - 4 min
Related Categories
Security
Update: We will be providing a Root Cause Analysis (RCA) with details in the coming weeks once our full investigation is complete.
What happened
On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.
What information was affected
The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:
Names and email addresses
Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times
Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)
Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)
Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery
Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)
The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.
When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning . During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.
What was not affected
Your vaults and the items in them
The keys that protect your vaults
1Password does not store your account password or secret key
Account recovery keys
1Password apps and browser extensions
What we’ve done
Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.
Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.
Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.
Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.
Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.
Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.
What you can do
Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.
Our commitment to you
You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.
We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

hn.text:
Skip to content
One minute
Install
BUI Charts is a set of components for BUI . Run this command below to use it in your project.
Terminal cargo add --git https://github.com/ppmpreetham/BUI blenderui bui-charts
Two minutes
Your first chart
A chart is a component. Write it in rsx! like any other tag, style it with class , and feed it from your own state. When the signal changes, the chart redraws.
src/dashboard.rs use blenderui :: prelude ::* ;
use bui_charts ::* ;
#[derive( Clone , PartialEq )]
struct Reading {
temperature : f64 ,
load : f64 ,
}
#[component]
fn dashboard () {
let readings = use_signal ( vec! [
Reading { temperature : 18 . , load : 32 . },
Reading { temperature : 24 . , load : 51 . },
Reading { temperature : 31 . , load : 77 . },
]);
rsx! {
<div class = "flex flex-col gap-4 p-4" >
< XYChart data = {readings} class = "h-72" >
< Series name = "Load" x = { | r : & Reading | r . temperature} y = { | r : & Reading | r . load} / >
< / XYChart >
< BarGauge data = {readings} value = { | r : & Reading | r . load} class = "h-16" / >
< / div>
}
}
Good to know
What every chart shares
Your data, your shape Pass a Vec , a Signal > or anything that implements Dataset . Charts read your rows through small closures like x={|r| r.load} , so you never reshape data for the chart.
Hover, legends and tooltips Hovering fades the rest and opens a tooltip. Clicking a legend entry hides that series and the chart re-scales. Every chart takes tooltip , legend and class .
Zoom and select Wheel and pinch zoom the plots that have axes. Drag to select a range where it makes sense.
Theming Charts read the colours of the active theme, so light, dark and your own palette all work without extra props.
Cheap to redraw Layouts are cached and only recomputed when the data, the size, the hidden set or the theme changes. Hovering does not re-layout.
Orientation
How these docs work
There are 7 base charts, the ones everything else is built on, and 73 derived charts that can help you visualize your data.
Since there are a lot of charts, here are a few pages you should probably visit next:
All charts Every chart as a picture. Filter by name or family. Which chart to use? Start from the question you want to answer. Domain specific Finance, electronics, biology, earth science and more.

hn.title: Curiosity Is No Solo Act
hn.text:
Curiosity Is No Solo Act
It gains its real power when embedded in webs of relationship and shared meaning-making.
MIT Press Reader/Source images: Adobe Stock By: Perry Zurn and Dani S. Bassett
A↑
A↓
Off
Bright
Dark
Blues
Gray
BeeLine Reader uses subtle color gradients to help you read more efficiently.
For millennia, curiosity has been characterized predominantly as an individual drive to acquire information. Whether it is Saint Augustine’s “lust to experience,” John Locke’s “appetite after knowledge,” Sigmund Freud’s “scopophilic drive,” or Hans-Georg Voss ’s “motivation to explore,” philosophers and psychologists of the Western intellectual tradition have largely understood curiosity at the level of the individual organism, its forces, and its feelings.
Perry Zurn and Dani S. Bassett are the authors of “ Curious Minds ,” from which this article is adapted.
But in the ancient and medieval periods, such expressions of individuality were also deeply suspect. Curiosity was seen as a largely vacuous interest in novel or forbidden information. The curious person was thought to reach for what was hidden and secret, beyond their proper purview, and thereby isolate themselves from spiritual and social community.
The accounts of Plutarch, a Roman essayist, and Augustine, a Christian bishop, are representative in this respect. For Plutarch, the curious person — or in his nomenclature, the busybody — was an oddball, a singular fellow, and a bit of an earwig. The busybody’s curiosity manifests as “a desire to learn” and “a passion to find out” what is truly new and novel. They push into the bazaars, marketplaces, and harbors asking, “Is there any news?” The busybody’s quest for maggoty mysteries is pursued without concern for themself or others. Abandoning their own interests and leaving their own soul in seedy squalor, the busybody jeopardizes their friendships and destroys social ties.
As an antidote to this “disease” of curiosity, then, Plutarch recommends a suite of ascetic practices, including not opening a letter upon its receipt, not consummating a marriage, and, upon hearing a theatrical performance in the distance, walking in the other direction. The message is simple: Abandon the singular secret, the devil in the details.
In the Bible, the curious person is in many ways similarly positioned as a sinner. Genesis begins, of course, with a story of creation and curiosity. The first woman, Eve, wants to partake of the one tree forbidden to her, representing the knowledge from which she and Adam are prohibited. Curious to know good and evil, she eats — that is, she reaches for, grasps, tugs, acquires, ingests, and consumes — a single piece of fruit from the forbidden tree, and her eyes are opened. Through her, all of humanity is condemned, metaphorically, to creep on its belly like a serpent, eating things worldly rather than spiritual.
The curious person was thought to reach for what was hidden and secret, beyond their proper purview.
While the hyperindividualized nature of curiosity and its interest in orphaned details is of the utmost concern in the ancient and medieval periods, these same characteristics are curiosity’s strongest commendations in the early modern period, in which scientific and philosophical inquiry set the stage for the Industrial Revolution.
René Descartes defined curiosity as a “desire to understand.” John Locke saw it as “an appetite after knowledge.” David Hume positioned curiosity as “the love of truth.” In the spirit of Francis Bacon, then, modern curiosity, performed by independent knowers, courted surprising information for its own sake, a process that itself ultimately served the cause of social utility. In other words, singularly curious objects inspired the individual practitioner of curiosity to gain knowledge that would be of eventual use to society.
The conceptualization of curiosity as an individual drive to discover something for society’s benefit persists today. But imagine a curiosity that is more social and praxiological than it is individual, intellectual, and acquisitional. Imagine a curiosity that aims less to know and more to make connections, build constellations, find links, and follow threads, functioning within a webbed network of relations between knowers, methods of knowing, and knowledges.
It is an intriguing suggestion at the very least, but is there historical precedent for such a concept? In short, yes.
Michael Foucault is a 20th-century thinker of power, specifically the power to resist established ways of thinking and doing. In a late interview, Foucault discusses this resistance as it relates to the queer community, which inherits a set of practices from the cisheteronormative world that includes settled ways of speaking, thinking, feeling, and relating both sexually and romantically. That is, there are well-worn pathways that typically define the romantic sagas of men and women.
In the face of those established networks, the task of queer people, Foucault suggests, is to “escape . . . [these] readymade formulas” and “invent” something still “improbable” — “way[s] of life” that traverse inherited formulas and institutionalized patterns. That is to say that queer life requires reconfiguring networks, revamping the ways a graph is walked.
To do so, queer people have to think and move in a “slantwise” direction, constantly creating “diagonal lines” in the social network. They must generate fresh forms of signification and sources of significance; they have to tell new stories. Ultimately, given that “what exists is far from filling all possible spaces,” the generation of more channels of information creates more chances for resistance and reconfiguration. With more fabric, there can be more fabrication.
The Foucauldian assumption that networks of information precondition ways of thinking, doing, and being has an ancient, rich, and still robust precedent in Indigenous philosophy. Rooted in the wisdom that everything that exists is connected

On June 9, 2026, we released the first production-ready version of Euro-Office , a sovereign collaborative office suite developed and governed in Europe. With Nextcloud Hub 26 Summer , we announced the release of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app powered by Euro-Office. Today, the ready-to-use version of the app is available for download. It lets you work offline, switch between Nextcloud Hub in your browser and the app on your computer, and get the same experience on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Download the app
In this article, you’ll learn about the app’s features, how to install it on Windows, macOS and Linux, and how to co-edit files with your team through Nextcloud Hub.
Free desktop office with maximum file compatibility
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app is a free and open source office suite for Windows, macOS and Linux. Featuring editors for text documents, spreadsheets, presentations, and PDFs, it offers high compatibility with Microsoft Office formats (DOCX, XLSX, PPTX) and open formats (ODT, ODS, ODP). Connect it to Nextcloud Hub to edit files with your team in real time.
The app includes the features of Nextcloud Office in your browser, plus the benefits of working on your computer:
Work offline and keep files on your device
Use the fonts installed on your computer
Sign documents digitally
Work with local and online files
With the Nextcloud Office Desktop app, you can edit files locally without an internet connection. Working locally, you keep access to your files and you can keep working when you don’t have internet connection or your online tools go down. You decide which files stay on your computer and which go to the cloud.
Need to access your online files? You can connect your Nextcloud instance to the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to access all the files available to you, and edit them on your own or with your team in real time.
How to connect the Nextcloud Office Desktop app to the cloud:
Click “+” in the “Clouds” section in the Home tab
Choose “Nextcloud“ and specify the URL of your instance
Log in with your credentials
Once connected, choose your Nextcloud instance from the list. You can connect more than one instance to one app to have access to multiple cloud working environments.
Use your own fonts
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app uses fonts installed on your machine, including corporate fonts and default fonts from your OS, like Microsoft fonts on Windows. You can install additional custom fonts any time. No need to bother your Nextcloud admins!
Note: if your collaborators don’t have the same font, they’ll see a fallback font in their version of the file.
Digital signatures and file protection
The Nextcloud Office Desktop app lets you use digital signatures to sign your documents, spreadsheets and presentations. A signature shows who signed a file and that nobody has changed it since. Go to Protection tab and add a signature via Signature feature.
Keep in mind that you need a digital certificate to sign documents. To obtain one, you can ask your IT team at work, or get one for personal use from a trusted provider. You can find providers approved in the EU in this list .
In the Protection tab, you can also set a password for a file, or limit what others can do: comment, fill in forms, or edit with tracked changes only.
How to install the Euro-Office desktop app
You can find and download the latest version of the Nextcloud Office Desktop app from our official installation page .
The app is available for:
Windows: x64, ARM64
Linux: .deb (Debian, Ubuntu), .rpm (Fedora)
macOS (Apple Silicon)
You can also find unsigned builds of Euro-Office desktop app and build the app from the source yourself by following the instructions on GitHub .
We want to keep improving the app. You are welcome to share any issues you find with our engineering team on GitHub.
Want to contribute to Euro-Office? Here’s how to get involved
Contributions are welcome! Whether it’s a bug report, a feature idea, a translation, or a pull request, here’s how to take part:
Found a bug or have an idea? Open an issue and describe what you ran into or what you’d like to see.
Want to contribute code? Fork the relevant component repo, make your change, and open a pull request. For build changes, see the build docs .
Want to help translate? Localization improvements are always appreciated — see the editors’ interface translations.
Please keep contributions compatible with the project’s AGPL v3 license.

NormalScript: A perfectly normal scripting language
hn.text:
Embeds as a library
A pure JavaScript package for Node ≥ 24 or Bun ≥ 1.4, with no WASM module, native addon, or isolate to wire up. Call Runtime.make, pass plain host functions, and run.
Small and fast
Scripts compile to bytecode and run on a compact virtual machine inside your process. There is no worker to spawn and nothing to boot, so a run starts when you call it and stops on timeoutMs or an AbortSignal.
Code mode and little scripts
An agent, user, or plugin writes one script that chains many host calls, with loops, branches, and Promise.all in between. Errors return a kind, a message, and optional suggestions.
A plain host API
Host.fn turns an ordinary function into a global. Host.namespace resolves large catalogs lazily. Host.durableFn keeps long work running across a suspend. StreamingResponse streams a response body.
Suspend, save, and resume
Suspend a waiting run with program.suspend(), save its state with toBytes(), and continue it with fromBytes() and runtime.resume(). Same build, same globals, same result.
A JavaScript subset, a simple API
Scripts are written in a modern, strict-mode subset of JavaScript: async functions, generators, classes, and top-level await and return. The host API is Promise-based, with the same names over Effect at /effect.

hn.text:
EastJet’s pre-tax profit plunged to £24m in its financial year ending in September, compared with £658m in the previous 12 months. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
EastJet’s pre-tax profit plunged to £24m in its financial year ending in September, compared with £658m in the previous 12 months. Photograph: Lisi Niesner/Reuters
EasyJet boss unable to rule out further job losses after profits collapse by 96%
Kenton Jarvis says rival airlines could go bust after Iran war drives sharp rises in fuel prices and hits travel demand
The boss of easyJet has said he cannot rule out further job cuts and predicted some rival airlines could go bust, after soaring fuel prices this year triggered a collapse in profits.
EasyJet’s pre-tax profit dropped 96% to £24m in its financial year ending in September, compared with £658m in the previous 12 months.
The airline, which has agreed to a £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity firm Apollo , said in July it had lost more money than expected during the spring, as the Iran war pushed up fuel prices and hit travel demand .
Kenton Jarvis, the chief executive of easyJet, said on Wednesday that the year was “challenging for airlines due to the Middle East conflict and its effect on demand and fuel prices, which materially impacted our financial performance”.
This month, it emerged that the airline was consulting on cutting up to 50 roles at its head office in Luton. EasyJet employs about 16,000 people around the world.
Jarvis said: “Will I rule out future [job cuts]? Of course not. This is a commercial business, so we will always look to optimise our cost base.”
He said the group continued to “look for ways to be more efficient” in its head office, adding that he had no plans for cuts to frontline staff such as cabin crew and pilots.
Jarvis said weaker airlines in Europe could face an existential threat from elevated fuel prices. EasyJet’s fuel bill rose by 11% – or £244m – to £2.5bn this year alone.
Surging fuel bills have pushed several airlines to collapse, such as Spirit in the US.
“There could be airline failures. It would not surprise me,” Jarvis said. “This will put a lot of pressure on airlines because the fuel increase is still stubbornly high and not all airlines are hedged.
“We could see some consolidation both from the flag carriers continuing on their acquisition trail, but also potentially with some market failures.”
skip past newsletter promotion
after newsletter promotion
While the company said it had hedged 70% of its fuel costs at just over $800 a metric tonne for the winter, and 54% hedged for the summer period at about $890, prolonged higher costs could feed into higher ticket prices.
“Clearly these fuel costs will put a lot of pressure on fares,” Jarvis said, although he added that it was unlikely they would rise by as much as 20% next year, as predicted by Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary .
“It will always be dependent on demand,” Jarvis said. “EasyJet will always look to have greater value fares.”
Many airlines have already reduced their flight schedules this winter to offset the impact of higher fuel prices. This month, the chief executive of Virgin Atlantic, Corneel Koster, said the airline would fly less than planned by “probably about 8% because of the cost of fuel” and “because of the drop in demand in the winter schedule”.

Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
hn.text:
Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow. I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all. SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders: - Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads)
- Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library) Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal under ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/. A couple of caveats up front:
- Dragging moves files by default (same as iCloud Drive, because it uses File Provider on the startup volume)—hold Option to copy.
- macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only (not physical devices). It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), signed and notarized, and installable via Homebrew: brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop
Just sharing in case others run into the same friction—feedback or PRs welcome!
